claim: The cryo-EM reconstruction of human SMG1-8-9 kinase complex bound to a UPF1 phosphorylation site reached an overall resolution of 2.9 Å.
source: Here, we present a cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) reconstruction of a human SMG1-8-9 kinase complex bound to a UPF1 phosphorylation site at an overall resolution of 2.9 Å.
evidence: The resolution is stated in the abstract and confirmed in the methods and results sections with supporting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: This structure provides the first snapshot of a human PIKK with a substrate-bound active site.
source: This structure provides the first snapshot of a human PIKK with a substrate-bound active site.
evidence: The manuscript presents structural data showing substrate binding in the active site, which is stated to be the first such observation for human PIKKs.

claim: SMG1 specifically phosphorylates Ser/Thr-containing motifs with a glutamine residue at position +1 and a hydrophobic residue at position -1.
source: Together with biochemical assays, it rationalizes how SMG1 and perhaps other PIKKs specifically phosphorylate Ser/Thr-containing motifs with a glutamine residue at position +1 and a hydrophobic residue at position -1, thus elucidating the molecular basis for phosphorylation site recognition.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data showing specific interactions and biochemical assays demonstrating phosphorylation specificity (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: PIKKs oversee translation machinery in the cytoplasm (mTOR, SMG1).
source: Specifically, PIKKs oversee translation machinery in the cytoplasm (mTOR, SMG1), or regulate DNA damage repair in the nucleus (ATM, ATR and DNA-PK) (Shimobayashi and Hall, 2014; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Yamashita, 2013; Yamashita et al., 2001; Blackford and Jackson, 2017; Elías-Villalobos et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: PIKKs regulate DNA damage repair in the nucleus (ATM, ATR and DNA-PK).
source: Specifically, PIKKs oversee translation machinery in the cytoplasm (mTOR, SMG1), or regulate DNA damage repair in the nucleus (ATM, ATR and DNA-PK) (Shimobayashi and Hall, 2014; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Yamashita, 2013; Yamashita et al., 2001; Blackford and Jackson, 2017; Elías-Villalobos et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: All PIKK family members except TRAPP/Tra1 are Ser/Thr-protein kinases.
source: With the exception of the enzymatically inactive TRAPP/Tra1, which serves as a scaffold in chromatin modification complexes, all other members of the PIKK family are Ser/Thr-protein kinases, and are among the largest proteins in the eukaryotic kinome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PIKK family members.

claim: TRAPP/Tra1 is enzymatically inactive and serves as a scaffold in chromatin modification complexes.
source: With the exception of the enzymatically inactive TRAPP/Tra1, which serves as a scaffold in chromatin modification complexes, all other members of the PIKK family are Ser/Thr-protein kinases, and are among the largest proteins in the eukaryotic kinome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about TRAPP/Tra1.

claim: Human SMG1 is one of the largest PIKK family members (~410 kDa).
source: Human SMG1 is one of the largest PIKK family members (~410 kDa) and plays a crucial role in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), a conserved pathway that regulates mRNA stability in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells (Kurosaki and Maquat, 2016; Karousis and Mühlemann, 2019).
evidence: The molecular weight is stated as a known property of SMG1.

claim: SMG1 plays a crucial role in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD).
source: Human SMG1 is one of the largest PIKK family members (~410 kDa) and plays a crucial role in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), a conserved pathway that regulates mRNA stability in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells (Kurosaki and Maquat, 2016; Karousis and Mühlemann, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NMD is a conserved pathway that regulates mRNA stability in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells.
source: Human SMG1 is one of the largest PIKK family members (~410 kDa) and plays a crucial role in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), a conserved pathway that regulates mRNA stability in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells (Kurosaki and Maquat, 2016; Karousis and Mühlemann, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In its canonical surveillance function, the NMD pathway recognizes and degrades aberrant mRNAs containing premature translation termination codons.
source: In its canonical surveillance function, the NMD pathway recognizes and degrades aberrant mRNAs containing premature translation termination codons, thus preventing the accumulation of truncated protein products.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NMD function.

claim: NMD regulates the levels of 5–10% of the transcriptome.
source: In addition, NMD also regulates the levels of a subset of normal, physiological transcripts, amounting to 5–10% of the transcriptome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about NMD's regulatory scope.

claim: In metazoans, SMG1 forms a stable complex with SMG8 and SMG9.
source: In metazoans, SMG1 forms a stable complex with two additional proteins, SMG8 and SMG9, and specifically phosphorylates the RNA helicase UPF1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is consistent with the experimental system used in the study.

claim: SMG1 specifically phosphorylates the RNA helicase UPF1.
source: In metazoans, SMG1 forms a stable complex with two additional proteins, SMG8 and SMG9, and specifically phosphorylates the RNA helicase UPF1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is confirmed by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Phosphorylation of UPF1 is a crucial event in the NMD pathway as it enables the recruitment of downstream NMD factors SMG5, SMG6 and SMG7.
source: Phosphorylation of UPF1 is a crucial event in this pathway as it enables the recruitment of downstream NMD factors SMG5, SMG6 and SMG7, leading to ribonucleolytic cleavage of the RNA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the NMD pathway mechanism.

claim: SMG1 phosphorylates UPF1 specifically at Ser/Thr - Gln (SQ) motifs present in the unstructured N- and C-terminal regions that flank the helicase core.
source: SMG1 phosphorylates UPF1 specifically at Ser/Thr - Gln (SQ) motifs present in the unstructured N- and C-terminal regions that flank the helicase core (Yamashita et al., 2001; Denning et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Specificity for a glutamine residue at the +1 position is shared by other PIKK family members, namely, ATM, ATR and DNA-PK kinases.
source: Specificity for a glutamine residue at the +1 position is shared by other PIKK family members, namely, ATM, ATR and DNA-PK kinases (Kim et al., 1999; Bannister et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Among the 20 possible SQ motifs in UPF1, only a selected few are effectively phosphorylated, including Ser1073, Ser1078, Ser1096 and Ser1116.
source: Among the 20 possible SQ motifs in UPF1, studies in vitro and in vivo have shown that only a selected few are effectively phosphorylated, including Ser1073, Ser1078, Ser1096 and Ser1116 (Yamashita et al., 2001; Ohnishi et al., 2003; Durand et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: UPF1 phosphorylation sites share a Leu-Ser-Gln (LSQ) consensus sequence identical to the LSQ consensus motif identified in substrates of the ATM kinase.
source: Interestingly, these UPF1 phosphorylation sites share a Leu-Ser-Gln (LSQ) consensus sequence identical to the LSQ consensus motif identified in substrates of the ATM kinase (O'Neill et al., 2000; Kim et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Purified SMG1-8-9 complex phosphorylated full-length recombinant UPF1 in a radioactive kinase assay.
source: The complex phosphorylated full-length recombinant UPF1 in a radioactive kinase assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), confirming the enzymatic activity of purified SMG1 towards its physiological substrate.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SMG1-8-9 specifically phosphorylates UPF1-LSQ peptide as confirmed by mass spectrometry-based phosphorylation assay.
source: We confirmed the ability of SMG1-8-9 to specifically phosphorylate UPF1-LSQ using a mass spectrometry-based phosphorylation assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Phosphorylation of UPF1-LSQ was abolished when Ser1078 was changed to Asp.
source: As a control, phosphorylation was abolished when Ser1078 was changed to Asp (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: SMG1 consists of an N-terminal solenoid 'arch' and a compact C-terminal 'head' region.
source: Briefly, SMG1 consists of an N-terminal solenoid 'arch' and a compact C-terminal 'head' region (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The C-terminal 'head' of SMG1 is formed by the tight interaction between the catalytic module and the FAT and FATC domains.
source: The C-terminal 'head' is formed by the tight interaction between the catalytic module, typical of Ser/Thr-kinases, and the so-called FAT and FATC domains (Imseng et al., 2018; Baretić and Williams, 2014; Bosotti et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data and citations to published literature.

claim: The N-terminal 'arch' of SMG1 provides binding sites for both SMG8 and SMG9.
source: The N-terminal 'arch' provides binding sites for both SMG8 and SMG9 (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: SMG9 contains an unusual G-fold domain that binds ATP rather than GTP or GDP.
source: As we had previously reported, SMG9 contains an unusual G-fold domain that binds ATP rather than GTP or GDP (Gat et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work by the same authors and confirmed by structural data in the current manuscript.

claim: The local resolution of around 3 Å allowed modeling of SMG9-bound ATP in the reconstructed density.
source: The local resolution of around 3 Å allowed us to model SMG9-bound ATP in the reconstructed density, revealing the molecular basis for how the adenosine nucleotide is recognized by this unusual G-fold domain (Figure 1B and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1B, D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The G4 and G5 motifs of SMG9 responsible for base recognition have rearranged to preferentially bind an adenine base rather than a guanine.
source: Another difference with canonical G-fold is that the G4 and G5 motifs responsible for the recognition of the base have rearranged to preferentially bind an adenine base rather than a guanine.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The current reconstruction revealed extra density in the kinase active site accounting for both AMPPNP and UPF1-LSQ compared to the previously published apo-SMG1-8-9 structure.
source: Importantly, compared to the previously published apo-SMG1-8-9 structure (Gat et al., 2019), the current reconstruction revealed extra density in the kinase active site accounting for both AMPPNP and UPF1-LSQ (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of structural data shown in Figure 1B, C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The active site of SMG1 shows excellent density for residues 1075–1081 of UPF1-LSQ.
source: The active site of SMG1 shows excellent density for residues 1075–1081 of UPF1-LSQ (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The directionality of the bound substrate peptide in SMG1 is consistent with that of other kinase structures, such as CDK2.
source: The directionality of the bound substrate peptide is consistent with that of other kinase structures, such as CDK2, and the arrangement of key active site residues is well conserved (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Bao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to published literature.

claim: The geometry of the catalytic loop and activation segment in the SMG1 kinase domain is very similar to those observed in mTOR, indicative of an active kinase state.
source: The geometry of the catalytic loop (residues 2332 to 2340) and of the activation segment (residues 2352 to 2375) in the SMG1 kinase domain as well as orientation of important active site residues are very similar to those observed in mTOR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), indicative of an active kinase state (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and citation to published literature.

claim: The hydroxyl group of Ser1078 is positioned by residues of the catalytic loop, in particular Asp2335 and His2337.
source: The hydroxyl group of Ser1078, the phospho-acceptor residue in UPF1-LSQ, is positioned by residues of the catalytic loop, in particular Asp2335 and His2337 (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 2B, C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutation of Asp2335 or His2337 in SMG1, mTOR and other protein kinases results in catalytically inactive enzyme.
source: Consistent with the structural observations, mutation of either of the corresponding residues in SMG1, mTOR and other protein kinases results in catalytically inactive enzyme (Bao et al., 2011; Madhusudan et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2013; Brown et al., 1995; Yamashita et al., 2001; Denning et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A glutamine residue following the phospho-acceptor site is the minimal requirement for UPF1 phosphorylation by SMG1.
source: A glutamine residue following the phospho-acceptor site is the minimal requirement for UPF1 phosphorylation by SMG1 (Figure 3A; Yamashita et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature and confirmed by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Only wildtype UPF1-LSQ was efficiently phosphorylated by SMG1 when the residue at position +1 was varied.
source: We changed the residue at position +1 in the UPF1-LSQ peptide to test the effect of different side chain properties on phosphorylation. Only wildtype UPF1-LSQ was efficiently phosphorylated by SMG1 (Figure 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: UPF1 Gln1079 stacks against Tyr3654 and Leu2365 and forms hydrogen bonds with the backbone of Val2367.
source: In particular, UPF1 Gln1079 stacks against Tyr3654 and Leu2365 and forms hydrogen bonds with the backbone of Val2367 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The hydrophobic cage for glutamine recognition is highly conserved in other PIKKs that recognize SQ motifs (ATM, ATR and DNA-PK) but is different in mTOR.
source: The hydrophobic cage is highly conserved in other PIKKs that recognize SQ motifs (ATM, ATR and DNA-PK) but is different in mTOR (where Glu2369 is found at the equivalent position of SMG1 Leu2365) (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: mTOR has been found to prefer small or non-polar residues at position +1 of its phosphorylation consensus motif.
source: Indeed, mTOR has been found to prefer small or non-polar residues at position +1 of its phosphorylation consensus motif (Hsu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The structural superposition with CtTel1ATM shows that its PIKK regulatory domain (PRD) places a Gln residue in the corresponding hydrophobic cage, effectively occupying the substrate Gln binding site.
source: Intriguingly, the structural superposition with CtTel1ATM shows that its PIKK regulatory domain (PRD) places a Gln residue in the corresponding hydrophobic cage, effectively occupying the substrate Gln binding site (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The PRD domain occupying the substrate Gln binding site explains the autoinhibitory function of the ATM PRD domain.
source: This explains the autoinhibitory function of the ATM PRD domain (Jansma et al., 2020; Yates et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on structural observations and supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The corresponding PRD domain in SMG1 is a ~ 1100 amino-acid long insertion that negatively impacts its kinase activity.
source: The corresponding PRD domain in SMG1 is a ~ 1100 amino-acid long insertion (Figure 1A) that negatively impacts its kinase activity (Deniaud et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature and structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There is no ordered density for the SMG1 PRD region in neither the previous apo-structure nor in the current substrate-bound structure.
source: However, there is no ordered density for this region in neither the previous apo-structure (Gat et al., 2019) nor in the current substrate-bound structure (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A and B and citation to previous work.

claim: SQ motifs preceded by a hydrophobic residue in position −1 are preferentially phosphorylated by SMG1.
source: Previous results have indicated that SQ motifs preceded by a hydrophobic residue in position −1 are preferentially phosphorylated by SMG1 (Yamashita et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The Leu residue at position −1 in the substrate forms a C-H⋅⋅⋅π-interaction with SMG1 Phe2215.
source: In our model, the Leu residue at position −1 in the substrate forms a C-H⋅⋅⋅π-interaction with SMG1 Phe2215 and is further stabilized by hydrophobic interactions with SMG1 Pro2249 and Gly3656.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SQ motifs carrying a hydrophobic residue in position −1 were more efficiently phosphorylated, with Leu eliciting the highest phosphorylation rate.
source: Following phosphorylation of the peptides over time, we could observe that SQ motifs carrying a hydrophobic residue in position −1 were more efficiently phosphorylated. Notably, a Leu elicited the highest phosphorylation rate (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Decreasing hydrophobicity of the residue at the −1 position negatively affects phosphorylation efficiency.
source: This is reflected at the biochemical level, whereby decreasing hydrophobicity of the residue at the −1 position negatively affects phosphorylation efficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The SQ motifs that carry rather hydrophobic residues at the −1 position reside exclusively in the UPF1 C-terminus.
source: Interestingly, further analysis of the final time points in the time course phosphorylation experiment showed that the SQ motifs that carry rather hydrophobic residues at the −1 position (and are therefore more efficiently phosphorylated) reside exclusively in the UPF1 C-terminus (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mutating Asp27 to Leu in the UPF1 N-terminus phosphorylation site Thr28 resulted in a gain-of-function effect in the phosphorylation assay.
source: We tested whether SMG1-8-9 phosphorylation activity toward this motif could be enhanced by changing the residue at position −1 from the naturally occurring Asp to a Leu. Indeed, mutating the residue upstream of this SQ motif (Asp27Leu) resulted in a gain-of-function effect in the phosphorylation assay (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The residues involved in the recognition of UPF1 Leu1077 have diverged in other PIKKs, suggesting that the details of −1 recognition will differ.
source: These findings are in agreement with data for ATM and ATR (Kim et al., 1999), although the residues involved in the recognition of UPF1 Leu1077 have diverged, suggesting that the details of −1 recognition will differ in other PIKKs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural data and citation to published literature.

claim: There are no extensive interactions between SMG1 and the peptide residues preceding or following the LSQ motif.
source: Finally, we do not observe extensive interactions between SMG1 and the peptide residues preceding or following the LSQ motif in our structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural observations.

claim: There was no marked effect on phosphorylation when the residue at position +2 of UPF1-LSQ was changed.
source: Consistently, we did not detect a marked effect on phosphorylation in a time course experiment where we changed the residue at position +2 of UPF1-LSQ (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The results elucidate the mechanism of phospho-acceptor recognition and explain the specificity for Ser-containing substrates with a glutamine downstream residue at position +1 and an upstream hydrophobic residue at position −1 (particularly Leu).
source: The results elucidate the mechanism of phospho-acceptor recognition, and explain the specificity for Ser-containing substrates with a glutamine downstream residue at position +1 and an upstream hydrophobic residue at position −1 (particularly Leu).
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined structural and biochemical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: These findings can be extrapolated to other PIKK members, such as ATM and ATR.
source: These findings can be extrapolated to other PIKK members, such as ATM and ATR, and suggest a specific mechanism for PRD function by acting as a pseudosubstrate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the structural and biochemical data combined with sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The findings suggest a specific mechanism for PRD function by acting as a pseudosubstrate.
source: These findings can be extrapolated to other PIKK members, such as ATM and ATR, and suggest a specific mechanism for PRD function by acting as a pseudosubstrate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from structural observations showing PRD occupying the substrate binding site.

claim: The results provide molecular insights into a key step of the NMD pathway.
source: Our results provide molecular insights into a key step of the NMD pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on the structural and biochemical data elucidating substrate recognition by SMG1.

claim: Phosphorylation was decreased when Ser was changed to Thr in the UPF1-LSQ peptide.
source: In addition, phosphorylation was decreased when Ser was changed to Thr, consistent with previous data for ATM, ATR and DNA-PK (Kim et al., 1999; O'Neill et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citation to published literature.

claim: Phosphorylation was abolished when Ser1081 was tested, confirming specificity toward the SQ motif at Ser1078.
source: Phosphorylation was abolished when the phospho-acceptor residue was changed from Ser to Asp. This shows Ser1081 was not recognized for phosphorylation and confirms specificity toward the SQ motif.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Large parts of the SMG1-8-9 complex including the kinase domain and the bound UPF1 peptide are resolved to around 3 Å.
source: Large parts of the complex including the kinase domain and the bound UPF1 peptide are resolved to around 3 Å.
evidence: The claim is supported by local resolution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The overall isotropy of the map is confirmed by a sphericity of 0.957.
source: Overall isotropy of the map is confirmed by a sphericity of 0.957 (out of 1) (Tan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D FSC analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and citation to the method.

claim: In the G4 motif of SMG9, the aspartic acid that specifically engages the guanine moiety in GTPases has diverged to an arginine residue.
source: In the G4 motif, the aspartic acid that specifically engages the guanine moiety in GTPases has diverged to an arginine residue.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison and sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4F.

claim: Asn372 in the SMG9 G4 motif has shifted so that it engages the side-chain carbonyl group to interact with the adenine amino group.
source: Instead, Asn372 in the SMG9 G4 motif has shifted so that it engages the side-chain carbonyl group to interact with the adenine amino group (compare panels A and B with C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: In the G5 motif of SMG9, the main-chain carbonyl and amine groups of Pro432 and Met434 form adenine-specific interactions.
source: In the G5 motif, the SAK consensus sequence in RAS and RHEB has diverged in SMG9, with the main-chain carbonyl and amine groups of the upstream residues, Pro432 and Met434, forming adenine-specific interactions (compare panels A and B with C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: The G1-G3 motifs of SMG9 coordinate the phosphate moieties of ATP, similarly to the corresponding motifs of canonical GTPases, but lack the typical residues crucial for catalysis.
source: The G1-G3 motifs of SMG9 coordinate the phosphate moieties of ATP, similarly to the corresponding motifs of canonical GTPases, but with an important exception, in that they lack the typical residues crucial for catalysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E.

claim: The SMG1 kinase contains features that have previously been associated with a model preferring the presence of a 'dissociative' transition state, such as a positive charge closely involved in β-phosphate coordination (K2155).
source: The SMG1 kinase contains features that have previously been associated with a model preferring the presence of a 'dissociative' transition state, such as a positive charge closely involved in β-phosphate coordination, namely K2155 (residue not shown) (Wang and Cole, 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on structural observations and citation to published literature on kinase mechanisms.

claim: Decreased phosphorylation of peptides with non-hydrophobic position −1 residues is not only caused by competition with more optimal substrates.
source: The results indicate that decreased phosphorylation of peptides with non-hydrophobic position −1 residues is not only caused by competition with more optimal substrates (compare assay shown in Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Density for the unmodelled, C-terminal part of SMG8 appeared in two 3D classes not used for the final reconstruction.
source: Density for the unmodelled, C-terminal part of SMG8 appearing in two other 3D classes not used for the final reconstruction is highlighted in magenta. This part of SMG8 has been suggested to contribute to kinase regulation (Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by data processing results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citation to published literature.

claim: The C-terminal part of SMG8 has been suggested to contribute to kinase regulation.
source: This part of SMG8 has been suggested to contribute to kinase regulation (Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.
